# Glassmaking and glassblowing (`glassmaking`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/materials.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Metallurgy & materials (`materials`)
- Deps: helped by alkali_soda, lime_burning, refractories_fireclay, charcoal_burning
- Core idea: A typical soda-lime glass contains three main oxides, supplied by sand or crushed quartz (about 65–70 %), an alkali that makes it melt (soda or plant ash, about 15–20 %) and lime (about 10 %) that makes it stand up to water. Roast the mixed batch for hours at dull red heat (fritting), then melt it in fireclay pots at 1100–1300 °C until the bubbles rise out. A gather taken on the end of an iron tube about 1.3 m long can be blown, swung and shaped while it stays orange-hot. Finished pieces must cool slowly over many hours in a chamber at about 500 °C, or they shatter later. Broken glass added to the batch helps it melt.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sand alone will not melt in any wood-fired furnace (it needs about 1700 °C).
  - Leaving out the lime gives a glass that clouds, weeps and finally dissolves in water.
  - Skipping the slow cooling; the piece cracks hours or days later, sometimes violently.
  - Ordinary sand contains iron and gives green or brown glass.
  - Pots that fail in the furnace; glassmaking stands or falls with the fireclay.
- History: mesopotamia: c. 2500 BC – first glass beads; c. 1500 BC core-formed vessels; c. 50 BC glassblowing invented on the Syro-Palestinian coast; egypt: c. 1500 BC – glass vessels and ingots (Amarna, Qantir); earlier faience; india: c. 1000 BC – glass beads; large bead industries by the last centuries BC; china: c. 5th–4th c. BC – lead-barium glass, a separate recipe; blown glass arrives with imports in the Han period; rome: 1st c. AD – blown vessels cheap and common; window panes; islamic: 8th–14th c. – plant-ash glass, cutting, lustre painting, enamelled and gilded glass in Syria and Egypt; africa: 11th–15th c. – glass made from local materials at Ile-Ife (Nigeria); europe: medieval potash 'forest glass'; 1291 Venetian furnaces moved to Murano; 1612 Neri prints the first book of glass recipes
- Read:
  - Antonio Neri, L'arte vetraria (1612)
  - Theophilus, De diversis artibus (c. 1120; tr. Hawthorne & Smith, On Divers Arts, 1963)
  - Julian Henderson, Ancient Glass: An Interdisciplinary Exploration (2013)
